To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

common SNPs explain a substantial fraction of the variance in complex traits, that the variance explained is approximately proportional to gene content, that cryptic relatedness can be estimated using common SNPs and that the variance explained can be used to infer the number of causal variants.
the variance in complex traits is partitioned into additive, dominance and epistasis components, and that the variance explained at each SNP is proportional to its minor allele frequency.
common SNPs explain a substantial amount of the genetic variance for complex traits, and that this amount of variance increases approximately in proportion to the length of the DNA in the region.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic architecture of common complex diseases and traits.
the genetic basis of common diseases, and in particular, the genetic basis of the variation in complex traits.
the partitioning of genetic variance for complex traits and diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the heritability of a trait is a property of the trait, and that the proportion of variance explained by common SNPs is a property of both the trait and the set of SNPs used in the analysis.
a large fraction of the variation in height, BMI and von Willebrand Factor can be accounted for by common SNPs.

the majority of genetic variation for these complex traits is captured by common variants, that these traits are highly polygenic, and that the variation explained by each part of the genome (chromosome) is proportional to the length of DNA therein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the heritability for complex traits is largely due to common SNPs.

the heritability of a complex trait is a function of the number and frequency of the variants contributing to the phenotype, and that the genetic variance is approximately proportional to gene content.
we have shown that a large fraction of the genetic variation in complex traits can be captured by common SNPS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the genetic basis for complex traits is highly polygenic and that a substantial proportion (45%) of the variation in height can be attributed to common SNPs.

a large proportion of the genetic variation for complex human traits can be explained by the additive effects of common SNPs, and that the proportion of variation that can be explained is approximately proportional to chromosome length.
a substantial fraction of the heritability for height, BMI, QTi and von Willebrand Factor can be captured by common SNPS.
